Administrators currently SSH into production VMs through bastion hosts with public IP addresses. Security wants to eliminate public IPs on all VMs, require identity-based and audited administrative access, and prevent anyone from adding public IPs again. What should the architect recommend?
Keep the bastions but restrict SSH to office IPs.
Use Cloud VPN for every administrator's laptop.
Assign public IPs only during maintenance.
Use IAP TCP forwarding for SSH and RDP, remove external IPs and bastions, and enforce the `compute.vmExternalIpAccess` organization policy.
IAP TCP forwarding provides identity-aware, audited access without public IPs, and the organization policy prevents reintroducing them.
Bastions with public IPs keep exposure, per-laptop VPN adds complexity, and temporary public IPs still create windows of exposure.

A healthcare company must detect and block known exploits and malware in east-west traffic between application tiers inside its VPC, using a Google-managed service rather than third-party appliances. What should the architect recommend?
Cloud NGFW Enterprise with intrusion prevention security profiles applied through network firewall policies, with firewall endpoints in the relevant zones.
Cloud NGFW Enterprise inspects traffic in-line and can block threats between workloads.
Cloud Armor protects traffic at load balancers, flow logs don't inspect payloads, and Cloud IDS detects but doesn't block.

A company wants the central security team to enforce baseline firewall rules across all VPCs, such as blocking known-bad ranges and allowing health checks, while delegating application-specific rules to each business unit's network team for its own folder. What should the architect design?
A single VPC firewall rule set copied into every VPC by the security team.

Hierarchical firewall policies at the organization level for the baseline, with `goto_next` for other traffic, folder-level policies for business units, and VPC-level policies managed by application teams.
Cloud Armor edge policies for internal traffic.
Hierarchical policies let the organization enforce non-overridable rules and delegate the rest to folder and VPC levels.
Copied rules can be modified locally, organization policies don't define firewall rules, and Cloud Armor isn't used for internal VPC traffic.

An internal HR application runs on Cloud Run. It must not be reachable from the internet at all, only from corporate users through an internal Application Load Balancer reached over Cloud Interconnect. What should the architect configure?
Set the Cloud Run service's ingress to allow internal traffic and Cloud Load Balancing only, and front it with an internal Application Load Balancer using a serverless NEG.
Keep the default ingress setting and require authentication.
Restrict access with a Cloud Armor policy on the default `run.app` URL.
Deploy the service in a private VPC subnet.
Cloud Run's ingress settings can block direct internet access, while an internal load balancer with a serverless NEG exposes the service privately to connected networks.
Default ingress allows internet reachability, Cloud Armor can't attach to the default URL, and Cloud Run services aren't deployed into subnets.

A bank is hardening a production GKE platform. Requirements: no public IPs on nodes, Pods authenticate to Google APIs without keys, node boot integrity is verified, and Pod-to-Pod traffic follows least-privilege rules. Which combination should the architect specify?
Public nodes with firewall rules, node service account keys, and default networking.
GKE Autopilot with public nodes and Kubernetes RBAC only.
Private nodes with Cloud NAT only.
Private nodes, Workload Identity Federation for GKE, Shielded GKE nodes with Secure Boot, and Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforced through GKE Dataplane V2.
Private nodes remove public exposure, Workload Identity Federation avoids keys, Shielded nodes verify boot integrity, and network policies restrict Pod traffic.
The other options leave public exposure, use keys, or omit Pod-level traffic controls.

A company with 400 projects wants a single place to detect misconfigurations such as public buckets and open firewall rules, identify vulnerabilities, detect active threats, and prioritize findings across the organization. What should the architect recommend?
Separate Cloud Monitoring dashboards per project.
Activate Security Command Center (Premium or Enterprise tier) at the organization level.
Weekly manual audits with gcloud scripts.
VPC Flow Logs in every project.
Security Command Center provides organization-wide posture management, vulnerability findings, and threat detection in one place.
Per-project dashboards and manual audits don't scale or detect threats, and flow logs are a data source rather than a security posture platform.

Security Command Center Event Threat Detection reports cryptocurrency mining on Compute Engine VMs a few times a month. The security team wants those VMs isolated automatically within minutes of a finding, with a notification to the on-call team. What should the architect design?

Configure a Security Command Center notification to Pub/Sub for the relevant finding categories, triggering a Cloud Run function that applies an isolating network tag or firewall rule, snapshots the disk, and notifies on-call.
Delete the entire project when a finding appears.
Disable Event Threat Detection to reduce noise.
Finding notifications through Pub/Sub enable automated, fast containment while preserving evidence.
Daily manual review is too slow, deleting projects destroys evidence and services, and disabling detection hides threats.

After a supply chain incident, a company wants to ensure that only container images built by its official CI pipeline and approved by security can run on its production GKE clusters and Cloud Run services. What should the architect implement?
Kubernetes RBAC restricting who can deploy.
Binary Authorization with policies requiring attestations created by the CI pipeline and security approval, enforced on production clusters and services.
Binary Authorization enforces deploy-time policies that permit only images with required attestations.
RBAC controls who deploys rather than what is deployed, cleanup policies manage storage, and network controls don't verify image provenance.

A platform team wants to prevent container images with critical vulnerabilities from reaching production, with vulnerabilities detected automatically when images are pushed and continuously as new CVEs are published. What should the architect design?
Monthly manual scans on developer laptops.
Use only official base images and skip scanning.

Enable Artifact Analysis vulnerability scanning in Artifact Registry, and in CI create a Binary Authorization attestation only if the image has no critical vulnerabilities, with production requiring that attestation.
Artifact Analysis scans images on push and as new vulnerabilities are published, and gating attestations on scan results blocks vulnerable images.
Manual scans are infrequent, runtime detection is too late to prevent deployment, and base images can still contain vulnerabilities.

A company's security operations center needs to ingest petabytes of logs from Google Cloud, on-premises firewalls, endpoint tools, and SaaS apps; retain them for a year; and run fast threat hunting and detection rules across all sources. What should the architect recommend?
Google Security Operations (SIEM) with ingestion from Google Cloud and third-party sources.
BigQuery tables queried manually by analysts.
Google Security Operations is a cloud SIEM built to ingest multi-source security telemetry at scale with long retention, detection rules, and threat hunting.
Default log buckets and manual BigQuery queries lack SIEM capabilities, and Monitoring alerts target metrics.

A production VM shows signs of compromise. The incident response team needs to stop further damage while preserving evidence for forensic analysis. What should the architect recommend as initial steps?
Delete the VM immediately and recreate it from the image.
Isolate the VM with restrictive firewall rules (for example, through an isolation tag), snapshot its disks for forensics, preserve relevant logs, and investigate before remediation.
Restart the VM to clear memory.
Grant the attacker's IP an allow rule to track activity.
Isolating the VM limits spread, while snapshots and logs preserve evidence for investigation.
Deleting or restarting destroys evidence, and allowing attacker traffic increases risk.

A financial services company must continuously demonstrate compliance with CIS benchmarks across its Google Cloud organization, detect configuration drift, and report posture to auditors. What should the architect recommend?
Security Command Center posture management with predefined security postures (such as CIS) deployed to the organization, and use its compliance reporting to track violations and drift.
Security postures in Security Command Center define and monitor benchmark-based controls, detect drift, and support compliance reporting.
Annual audits and pre-audit scripts don't provide continuous monitoring, and billing reports are unrelated to compliance.

A regulated bank requires visibility into any access to its data by Google personnel and wants the ability to explicitly approve or deny such access before it occurs for supported services. What should the architect enable?
Cloud Audit Logs Data Access logs only.
Access Transparency logs and Access Approval.
Access Transparency records actions taken by Google personnel on customer content, and Access Approval requires explicit customer approval before such access.
Data Access logs record customer principals' access, VPC Service Controls restricts API access paths, and EKM controls keys rather than approving personnel access.

A company deploys public web applications on App Engine, Compute Engine, and GKE and wants automated scanning of these applications for common vulnerabilities such as cross-site scripting and outdated libraries before and after releases. What should the architect recommend?
Web Security Scanner, integrated with Security Command Center.
Web Security Scanner crawls web applications to identify vulnerabilities such as XSS and outdated libraries and reports findings to Security Command Center.
Cloud Armor filters traffic rather than scanning apps, flow logs show network flows, and Binary Authorization controls image deployment.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A retail startup must launch a loyalty program in eight weeks to match a competitor. The engineering team of six proposes building a custom message queue, a custom identity system, and a self-managed database cluster to keep full control. The CEO's top priority is time to market, and the team has limited operations experience. What should the architect recommend?
Use managed services such as Pub/Sub, Identity Platform, and Cloud SQL so the team focuses on business features rather than infrastructure.
Build the custom components as proposed and delay the launch if needed.
Outsource all development to a contractor.
Build a minimal version on a single VM with no redundancy.
Managed services reduce build and operations effort, aligning with the time-to-market priority and the team's limited operations experience.
Custom infrastructure delays launch and adds operational risk, outsourcing doesn't address platform choice, and a single VM creates reliability risks for a customer-facing program.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A SaaS company's contract promises customers 99.9% monthly availability with service credits if missed. The engineering team wants to know how to set its internal reliability target. What should the architect recommend?
Set the internal SLO equal to the SLA at 99.9%.
Set the internal SLO lower than the SLA, at 99.5%, to reduce engineering effort.
Set an internal SLO stricter than the SLA (for example, 99.95%) so that the team responds before customers are affected and credits are owed.
Don't set an SLO; track only the SLA.
An internal SLO tighter than the contractual SLA gives a buffer to detect and fix problems before breaching the agreement.
Matching the SLA leaves no margin, a looser SLO guarantees breaches, and tracking only the SLA gives no early warning.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
An e-commerce company wants an SLI for its checkout experience that reflects what customers care about: purchases that succeed quickly. Which SLI is most appropriate?
Average CPU utilization of checkout VMs.
The proportion of checkout requests, measured at the load balancer, that return a successful response within 300 ms.
The number of checkout VMs running.
A good SLI measures user-facing outcomes, such as the ratio of successful and fast requests, ideally close to the user at the load balancer.
CPU, VM counts, and disk usage are internal resource metrics that don't directly reflect customer experience.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A board approved a cloud migration expecting "better agility and lower costs." Twelve months later, the board asks whether the migration succeeded, but no one can answer objectively. What should the architect have established at the start?
The total number of Google Cloud services used.
Measurable KPIs with baselines, such as deployment frequency, lead time for changes, cost per transaction, and availability, tracked before and after migration.
Defining baseline and target KPIs tied to business goals allows objective evaluation of outcomes such as agility and cost efficiency.
Server counts and service counts measure activity rather than outcomes, and the bill alone ignores business value and volume changes.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company's steady baseline workload uses about 200 vCPUs around the clock, with seasonal peaks of up to 600 vCPUs for a few weeks a year. The CFO wants predictable spending and discounts, while engineering wants flexibility for peaks. What should the architect recommend?
Committed use discounts sized to the steady baseline, with on-demand (or Spot, where appropriate) capacity for peaks through autoscaling.
Commitments for 600 vCPUs to cover peaks.
On-demand pricing only, for maximum flexibility.
Spot VMs for all workloads, including the baseline.
Committing to the baseline captures discounts and predictability, while autoscaled on-demand capacity handles temporary peaks.
Committing to peak capacity wastes money most of the year, on-demand only forgoes discounts, and Spot VMs are unsuitable for interruption-sensitive baseline workloads.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company is modernizing web applications into containers. Its operations team has strong Linux skills but no Kubernetes experience, and leadership wants to start delivering value within one quarter while building skills over time. What should the architect recommend?
Build a self-managed Kubernetes cluster on Compute Engine to learn the internals.
Delay modernization until the team is fully certified in Kubernetes.
Start with Cloud Run for stateless services while training the team, adopting GKE later for workloads that need Kubernetes features.
Deploy everything to GKE Standard immediately with default settings.
Cloud Run delivers containerized services quickly with minimal platform skills, while training prepares the team for GKE when needed.
Self-managed Kubernetes and immediate GKE Standard adoption add risk given the skills gap, and waiting delays business value.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

An insurance company receives 50,000 claim forms per month as PDFs and scanned images and wants structured data extracted into its claims system. A team proposes collecting labeled data and training a custom OCR model from scratch over six months. What should the architect recommend first?
Hire a team to enter data manually.
Evaluate Document AI processors (including specialized or custom extractors) to extract fields with minimal custom model development.
Train a custom OCR model on Compute Engine GPUs.
Store the PDFs in Cloud Storage and search them with keywords.
Document AI provides managed document processing that can be adapted to specific forms, reducing time and cost compared with building from scratch.
Manual entry doesn't scale, a custom OCR model is slow and costly, and keyword search doesn't produce structured data.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A European fintech wants the lowest possible latency for trading users in Singapore, and product managers propose storing customer account data in `asia-southeast1`. However, EU regulations applying to the company require that this personal data stay in the EU. How should the architect resolve the conflict?
Store the data in Singapore because latency affects revenue.
Store data in both regions and hope regulators don't notice.
Choose the region with the lowest cost.
Treat data residency as a hard constraint; keep personal data in the EU and reduce latency through other means, such as edge caching of non-personal content and optimized application design.
Regulatory requirements are non-negotiable constraints, so the design must optimize latency within them.
Violating residency for performance or cost creates legal risk, and duplicating data outside the EU still breaches the requirement.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A large enterprise's cloud adoption has stalled: teams use Google Cloud inconsistently, security is ad hoc, and leadership lacks a clear roadmap. The CIO asks the architect how to assess the organization's cloud maturity and plan next steps. What should the architect use?
The Google Cloud Adoption Framework, assessing maturity across themes such as Learn, Lead, Scale, and Secure to create a prioritized roadmap.
A list of Google Cloud services the company doesn't yet use.
A migration plan for all remaining servers.
The Cloud Adoption Framework evaluates people, process, and technology maturity across themes and guides a roadmap.
A service list or server migration plan doesn't address organizational maturity, and cost reduction alone ignores skills, leadership, and security.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A traditional bank's executives are nervous about moving to the cloud, and several teams resist change. The architect needs to build confidence and demonstrate value early with limited risk. What should the architect recommend?
Migrate the core banking system first to show commitment.
Mandate that all teams migrate within three months.
Select a lighthouse project, such as a non-critical but visible workload, deliver it successfully, share lessons learned, and use it to build skills and patterns for later waves.
Wait until competitors have fully migrated.
A lighthouse project provides a low-risk, visible success that builds skills, reusable patterns, and organizational confidence.
Starting with the core system is high risk, mandates fuel resistance, and waiting forfeits advantage.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
A product manager asks how much downtime per 30-day month is allowed by a 99.9% availability target. What's the closest answer?
0.1% of 30 days (43,200 minutes) is about 43.2 minutes.
About 4.3 minutes corresponds to 99.99%, and 7.2 hours corresponds to 99%.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A customer-facing API depends on three serially dependent components, each with 99.95% availability, and any single failure makes the API unavailable. The business wants to promise 99.95% availability for the API. What should the architect advise?
The API's availability is 99.95%, because it matches its components.
The API's availability is the highest of the components.
Availability can't be estimated for dependent systems.
The expected availability is roughly 99.85% (0.9995³), so meeting 99.95% requires adding redundancy or removing hard dependencies.
Availabilities of serial dependencies multiply, lowering the composite availability below each component's.
Achieving the target requires redundancy, graceful degradation, or fewer hard dependencies, so the other options misstate how availability composes.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
A ticketing company expects traffic to spike to 20 times normal levels when a major concert goes on sale next month. It has never tested at that scale. What should the architect recommend first?
Run load tests that simulate expected peak traffic in a production-like environment, identify bottlenecks such as database connections and quotas, and fix them before the sale.
Double all resources the night before the sale.
Enable Cloud CDN for all API calls.
Load testing reveals bottlenecks like database limits, quotas, and scaling delays before real users are affected.
Blind resource increases may miss the true bottleneck, untested autoscaling can hit limits, and CDN doesn't help with dynamic, personalized API calls.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A news website's Cloud SQL primary is at 95% CPU, driven mainly by repeated reads of the same popular articles. Write volume is low. The team wants to reduce latency and database load without changing the database engine. What should the architect recommend?
Scale the primary vertically to the largest machine type.
Add Cloud SQL read replicas for read traffic and a Memorystore cache for popular articles.
Increase the Cloud SQL disk size.
Read replicas offload reads, and caching serves repeated requests from memory, both targeting a read-heavy bottleneck.
Vertical scaling has limits and cost, Spanner is a major change not justified by read load, and disk size doesn't address CPU.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company's image-processing service on GKE uses far more CPU than expected, raising costs. Engineers suspect inefficient code but don't know which functions are responsible. They want continuous, low-overhead analysis in production. What should the architect recommend?
Use Cloud Profiler to continuously profile CPU and memory usage by function in production.
Cloud Profiler collects low-overhead CPU and heap profiles from production and shows which functions consume resources.
Larger nodes increase cost without fixing code, logging doesn't reveal CPU hotspots effectively, and flow logs show network traffic.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

Users report that a request passing through eight microservices sometimes takes more than five seconds. Each team says its own service is fast. The architect needs to find which call contributes the latency. What should the architect use?
Cloud Monitoring CPU charts for each service.
Distributed tracing with Cloud Trace (for example, via OpenTelemetry instrumentation) to see per-span latency across services.
Distributed tracing follows a request across services and shows the time spent in each span, identifying the slow dependency.
CPU charts, error metrics, and uptime checks don't reveal where latency accumulates within a request path.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A managed instance group serving a web application takes about four minutes for new VMs to become ready. Every morning, traffic ramps up quickly at 8 AM, and users see errors before the autoscaler catches up. What should the architect recommend?
Configure an appropriate initialization period and enable predictive autoscaling so capacity is added ahead of the recurring daily ramp.
Disable autoscaling and run at maximum capacity all day.
Reduce the autoscaling target utilization to 5%.
Predictive autoscaling uses historical load patterns to scale out before predictable ramps, compensating for long startup times.
Running at maximum wastes money, an extremely low target is wasteful and still reactive, and Spot VMs don't speed scaling.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company's GKE Standard clusters run at about 30% average node utilization. Many Pods have inflated resource requests, and some batch workloads could tolerate interruptions. The company wants to reduce costs without harming critical services. What should the architect recommend?
Buy committed use discounts for the current node count.
Rightsize Pod requests using VPA recommendations, use the cluster autoscaler's optimize-utilization profile, and move interruption-tolerant batch workloads to Spot node pools.
Move all workloads to one large node.
Accurate requests improve bin-packing, the optimize-utilization profile scales down more aggressively, and Spot nodes reduce costs for tolerant workloads.
Commitments lock in waste, disabling autoscaling increases idle capacity, and a single node creates reliability risk.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

Executive dashboards in Looker Studio query a 20 TB BigQuery table every few minutes, scanning the full table each time. Costs are high, and dashboards are slow. The dashboards aggregate data by day and region. What should the architect recommend?
Create materialized views for the aggregations (and consider BI Engine), ensure queries select only needed columns, and filter on partitioned date columns.
Export the table to Cloud SQL for dashboards.
Duplicate the table for each dashboard.
Materialized views precompute aggregations, BI Engine accelerates interactive queries, and column selection with partition filters reduce bytes scanned.
More refreshes increase cost, Cloud SQL isn't suited to 20 TB analytics, and duplicate tables add cost.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A Cloud Run service scales to several hundred instances during peaks, each opening its own connections to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The database hits its connection limit, causing errors, although CPU remains moderate. What should the architect recommend?
Remove all maximum instance limits on Cloud Run.
Switch to a public IP for the database.
Introduce connection pooling (for example, Cloud SQL managed connection pooling or PgBouncer), limit connections per instance, and set a sensible maximum number of Cloud Run instances.
Pooling multiplexes many client connections over fewer database connections, and limiting instances and per-instance connections keeps totals within database limits.
Disk size and IP type don't affect connection limits, and removing instance limits makes exhaustion worse.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company maintains 15 small Compute Engine VMs whose only purpose is to run cron scripts once a day, each taking less than 10 minutes. The VMs require patching and cost money around the clock. What should the architect recommend?
Package the scripts as containers and run them as Cloud Run jobs triggered by Cloud Scheduler.
Consolidate all scripts onto one larger VM.
Keep the VMs and buy committed use discounts.
Move the scripts to GKE Standard with dedicated nodes.
Scheduled Cloud Run jobs eliminate always-on VMs and patching, charging only while jobs run.
One larger VM still requires management and idle cost, commitments lock in waste, and a dedicated GKE cluster adds overhead for simple jobs.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

An application writes millions of small log objects per hour to a Cloud Storage bucket using names such as `2026-09-30-10-00-00-000001.log`, `2026-09-30-10-00-00-000002.log`. During bursts, the application sees increased latency and occasional request errors from Cloud Storage. What should the architect recommend?
Switch the bucket to Archive class.
Add a random or hashed prefix to object names to distribute load across the key range, and ramp request rates gradually.
Reduce the object size to 1 KB.
Sequential names concentrate requests on a narrow key range, which can create hotspots during rapid ramps; randomized prefixes spread load.
Storage class and versioning don't affect request distribution, and smaller objects increase request counts.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A research institute runs thousands of containerized simulation jobs each week, some needing GPUs. Researchers currently create and delete VMs by hand, leaving idle VMs running for days. The institute wants a managed service that queues jobs, provisions the right resources, and cleans up automatically. What should the architect recommend?
A permanent GKE Standard cluster sized for peak.
Cloud Run functions for each simulation.
Cloud Scheduler with scripts that create VMs.
Batch, which schedules, provisions, and deletes compute resources for batch jobs, including GPU and Spot VMs.
Batch is a managed service that queues jobs, provisions VMs with the required resources, and cleans them up after completion.
A permanent peak-sized cluster wastes capacity, functions have time and resource limits unsuitable for long GPU jobs, and scripts recreate the manual problem.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company has committed to reducing the carbon footprint of its cloud workloads. It runs large batch analytics jobs that aren't latency sensitive and can run in any North American region. What should the architect recommend?
Run the jobs in the region closest to headquarters regardless of energy mix.
Run the jobs continuously to avoid startup emissions.
Run the jobs in regions with a higher carbon-free energy percentage, and use the Carbon Footprint report to measure progress.
Use larger machine types to finish faster.
Choosing low-carbon regions for flexible workloads reduces emissions, and Carbon Footprint reporting tracks progress.
Proximity to headquarters doesn't matter for batch work, continuous running wastes energy, and bigger machines don't necessarily lower emissions.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

During migration planning, an architect finds that an internal reporting application hasn't been used by anyone in 14 months, but it still runs on three on-premises servers with expensive licenses. What migration strategy should the architect recommend for this application?
Retire it after confirming with stakeholders, and archive any required data.
Unused applications should be retired, eliminating migration effort and licensing cost, with data archived if retention is required.
Rehosting, refactoring, or buying a replacement spends money on something no one uses.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company plans to migrate 2,000 on-premises servers and needs to discover inventory, collect utilization data, map dependencies, and estimate Google Cloud costs before building a business case. What should the architect use?
Manual spreadsheets filled in by each application owner.
Migration Center to discover assets, collect performance data, and generate cost estimates and migration recommendations.
Cloud Asset Inventory on on-premises servers.
Migration Center discovers and assesses on-premises infrastructure, including utilization, and produces cost and migration planning outputs.
Spreadsheets are incomplete, Asset Inventory tracks Google Cloud resources, and the Pricing Calculator requires already-known specifications.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

An online retailer must migrate a 3 TB MySQL database from its data center to Cloud SQL for MySQL. The business allows at most 10 minutes of downtime during cutover. What should the architect recommend?
Export a mysqldump, import it into Cloud SQL, and cut over.
Copy the raw database files to Cloud Storage and restore them manually.
Rebuild the database from application logs.
Use Database Migration Service with continuous replication from the source to Cloud SQL, then promote the destination during a short cutover window.
DMS performs an initial load followed by continuous change replication, so cutover requires only a brief promotion.
A one-time dump and import of 3 TB takes far longer than 10 minutes of downtime, raw file copies aren't a supported migration path to Cloud SQL, and rebuilding from logs is impractical.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company wants to move off an expensive Oracle database to a PostgreSQL-compatible managed database with high performance. It needs help converting schemas and code objects and wants to minimize downtime during migration. What should the architect recommend?
Database Migration Service for Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, using a conversion workspace to convert schema and code, followed by continuous replication and cutover.
Rehost Oracle on Compute Engine and keep the licenses.
Export Oracle tables to CSV and load them into BigQuery.
Rewrite the entire application before migrating any data.
DMS supports heterogeneous Oracle migrations to PostgreSQL-compatible targets, with conversion workspaces for schema and code and continuous replication to limit downtime.
Rehosting keeps licensing costs, BigQuery isn't a transactional replacement, and a full rewrite first delays benefits.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company wants to modernize a large, business-critical monolith into microservices, but a full rewrite is considered too risky. The business must keep shipping features during modernization. What approach should the architect recommend?
Freeze all feature development and rewrite the monolith in one release.
Rehost the monolith and never modernize.
Apply the strangler fig pattern: route traffic through a facade, incrementally extract capabilities into new services, and retire corresponding monolith parts over time.
Split the monolith's database into separate databases first, without changing code.
The strangler fig pattern replaces functionality incrementally while the system keeps running, reducing risk and allowing continued delivery.
A big-bang rewrite is risky, never modernizing ignores the goal, and splitting the database without code changes breaks the application.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company has dozens of Linux-based Java web applications running on VMs. It wants to move them to GKE to standardize operations and improve density, without rewriting code or manually writing Dockerfiles and Kubernetes manifests for each. What should the architect recommend?
Rewrite each application as a Cloud Run function.
Use Migrate to Containers to extract the applications from VMs into container images and generate Kubernetes deployment artifacts.
Rehost the VMs on Compute Engine and run kubectl on them.
Build container images manually for each application.
Migrate to Containers automates converting VM-based workloads into containers and Kubernetes artifacts, supporting replatforming without rewrites.
Rewriting as functions is a refactor, rehosting doesn't containerize, and manual builds are slow at this scale.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A retailer is migrating a 200 TB Teradata data warehouse to BigQuery. It has thousands of SQL scripts and reports written in Teradata SQL. What should the architect recommend to reduce migration effort?
Keep Teradata and replicate data to BigQuery forever.
Export data to Cloud Storage and query it with external tables only.
Use the BigQuery Migration Service, including its SQL translator for Teradata SQL, alongside data transfer tooling for the data.
BigQuery Migration Service provides assessment, SQL translation, and migration tooling that automate much of the conversion.
Manual rewriting is slow, permanent dual running is costly, and external tables alone don't migrate the warehouse or its logic.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company is planning migration waves for 150 applications. The first wave moved an order application to Google Cloud while its tightly coupled inventory service stayed on-premises. Chatty calls across the hybrid link caused severe latency. How should the architect plan future waves?
Use dependency mapping to group tightly coupled applications and their data into the same wave, and move them together.
Migrate the largest applications first regardless of dependencies.
Add bandwidth to the hybrid connection and keep the current wave plan.
Grouping interdependent applications prevents latency-sensitive calls from crossing hybrid links during the transition.
Alphabetical or size-based ordering ignores dependencies, and more bandwidth doesn't fix per-call latency for chatty interactions.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company is cutting over its core database from on-premises to Cloud SQL for a weekend. Leadership insists on the ability to roll back to on-premises within hours if serious problems appear in the first days, without losing transactions made in the cloud. What should the architect include in the plan?
Delete the on-premises database immediately after cutover.
Take one backup before cutover and restore it if needed.
After cutover, set up reverse replication from Cloud SQL to the on-premises database so it stays current, and define clear rollback criteria and procedures.
Run both databases independently and reconcile later.
Reverse replication keeps the old system current so rollback doesn't lose new transactions, and defined criteria make the decision clear.
Deleting the source removes rollback, a pre-cutover backup loses post-cutover data, and independent writes create conflicts.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company must migrate 500 TB of files from on-premises NAS to Cloud Storage. Files keep changing during the three-week migration, and cutover downtime must be short. The company has a 10 Gbps Interconnect. What should the architect recommend?
One `gcloud storage cp` run at the start of the migration.
Storage Transfer Service with on-premises agents for an initial bulk transfer, followed by incremental transfers of changes, and a final short incremental sync at cutover.
Transfer Appliance only, with no incremental updates.
Email files to the cloud team.
Storage Transfer Service handles large transfers over the available link, and incremental runs capture changes so the final sync is short.
A single copy misses changes, an appliance alone doesn't capture ongoing changes, and emailing files isn't viable.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

A company runs 800 VMs on VMware vSphere and must exit its data center within four months. Its operations team relies heavily on vCenter, NSX, and existing VMware runbooks, and wants to keep them during the move before modernizing. What should the architect recommend?
Convert every VM to Compute Engine images by hand.
Migrate the VMs to Google Cloud VMware Engine using VMware tools such as HCX, keeping existing operational processes.
Google Cloud VMware Engine runs native VMware stacks in Google Cloud, allowing fast migration with existing tools and runbooks.
Refactoring takes too long, manual conversion is slow and changes operations, and retiring all workloads isn't realistic.
4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes

Three months after rehosting 300 VMs to Compute Engine with the same sizes they had on-premises, the monthly bill is 40% higher than forecast. Utilization data shows most VMs are heavily overprovisioned. What should the architect recommend?
Apply rightsizing recommendations based on observed utilization, adjust machine types (including custom types), and then evaluate committed use discounts for the right-sized baseline.
Buy three-year commitments for the current VM sizes immediately.
Add more VMs to spread the load.
Post-migration optimization should rightsize based on real utilization before committing, avoiding locking in waste.
Committing to oversized VMs increases waste, repatriation ignores the fixable cause, and adding VMs increases cost.

Developers building a Pub/Sub- and Firestore-based application run integration tests against shared cloud projects. Tests are slow, interfere with each other, and generate unnecessary cost. The team wants fast, isolated local testing. What should the architect advise?
Give each developer their own production project.
Use the Pub/Sub and Firestore emulators (for example, through the gcloud CLI) for local development and unit or integration tests, with a smaller set of tests against real services in CI.
Mock all Google Cloud client libraries by hand.
Emulators provide fast, isolated, no-cost local testing, while a targeted set of CI tests validates behavior against real services.
Personal production projects add cost and risk, skipping tests reduces quality, and hand-written mocks often drift from real service behavior.

A bank's security team prohibits storing source code on developer laptops, and onboarding new developers currently takes a week of environment setup. Developers need consistent environments with approved tools and private access to internal repositories. What should the architect recommend?
Virtual desktop images shipped on USB drives.
Shared Compute Engine VMs with one account for all developers.
Let developers use personal laptops with disk encryption.
Cloud Workstations with standardized, administrator-managed configurations running inside the company's VPC.
Cloud Workstations provides managed, consistent development environments in the company's VPC, keeping source code off laptops and speeding onboarding.
USB images and personal laptops still place code on endpoints, and shared accounts remove accountability.

Build pipelines frequently fail due to rate limits when pulling base images from Docker Hub and packages from public npm and Maven repositories. Security also wants a controlled point through which third-party dependencies enter builds. What should the architect recommend?
Artifact Registry remote repositories that proxy and cache Docker Hub, npm, and Maven, with builds configured to use them (optionally combined with virtual repositories).
Increase the number of build retries.
Download packages manually and commit them to Git.
Use a different public registry for each build.
Remote repositories cache upstream artifacts, reducing rate-limit failures and providing a governed ingress point for dependencies.
Retries don't fix rate limits, committing packages to Git bloats repositories, and switching registries doesn't add control.

A product team uses long-lived feature branches that are merged every six weeks, causing painful merge conflicts and big-bang releases. Business stakeholders want to control when features become visible to customers independently of code deployments. What should the architect advise?
Lengthen release cycles to three months.
Require a single developer to integrate all branches.
Adopt trunk-based development with small, frequent merges, and use feature flags to separate deploying code from releasing features.
Trunk-based development reduces merge conflicts, and feature flags let the business decide when features go live without redeploying.
Longer cycles worsen integration pain, a single integrator becomes a bottleneck, and laptop deployments bypass controls.

A company runs a web application on a managed instance group behind a global external Application Load Balancer. It needs releases with instant rollback and the ability to test the new version in production-like conditions before switching all traffic. What deployment strategy should the architect recommend?
Blue/green deployment with two MIGs (current and new) as separate backend services, switching the URL map from blue to green after validation and back if needed.
Recreate all instances in place during a maintenance window.
Deploy directly on running VMs using SSH scripts.
Blue/green keeps the old environment running, so traffic can be switched after testing and switched back instantly.
Replacing everything at once, recreating in place, or patching live VMs doesn't provide instant rollback.

A logistics company exposes a public API to hundreds of partner integrations. The team needs to make breaking changes to response formats but can't force all partners to update at once. What should the architect advise?
Change the existing API in place and notify partners afterward.
Maintain separate deployments for each partner.
Introduce a new API version (for example, `/v2`) for breaking changes, keep `/v1` stable with a published deprecation timeline, and prefer backward-compatible changes where possible.
Explicit versioning with a deprecation policy lets partners migrate on their own schedule while enabling evolution.
In-place breaking changes cause outages, freezing blocks progress, and per-partner deployments are unmanageable.

A team deploys application updates with rolling updates on GKE, so old and new versions run simultaneously for several minutes. A new release requires renaming a database column, and the last attempt broke old Pods during the rollout. What should the architect advise?
Use the expand-and-contract pattern: add the new column and write to both, deploy code that reads the new column, backfill, and remove the old column in a later release.
Rename the column during the deployment and accept errors.
Stop all traffic during every schema change.
Store all data as JSON blobs to avoid schemas.
Expand-and-contract keeps the schema compatible with both old and new code during rollouts, enabling zero-downtime changes.
Accepting errors or stopping traffic hurts users, and abandoning schemas creates other data quality problems.

Fifty development teams each build their own deployment pipelines, logging setups, and GKE configurations, leading to inconsistent security and slow onboarding. Platform leadership wants teams to move fast while following standards. What should the architect recommend?

Build golden paths through an internal developer platform: reusable templates for services, pipelines, and infrastructure with security and observability built in, while allowing justified deviations.
Centralize all deployments through one operations team.
Golden paths make the secure, standard approach the easiest one, improving consistency and speed.
Documents alone are often ignored, full independence perpetuates inconsistency, and centralizing all deployments creates bottlenecks.

A company's Cloud Build pipelines must deploy to private GKE clusters with no public control plane endpoint and pull dependencies from an on-premises artifact server over Interconnect. Default Cloud Build workers can't reach these private resources. What should the architect recommend?
Enable public endpoints on the GKE clusters.
Use Cloud Build private pools peered with the VPC so builds can reach private resources.
Run builds on developers' laptops over VPN.
Copy the on-premises artifact server to a public bucket.
Private pools run build workers in a Google-managed network connected to your VPC, enabling access to private endpoints and hybrid resources.
Public endpoints and public buckets increase exposure, and laptop builds lose consistency and control.

A software vendor's enterprise customers require verifiable evidence of how each container image was built, including the source revision and build steps, aligned with SLSA. What should the architect advise the development team to implement?
Include a README in each image.
Store build logs on a shared drive.
Tag images with the developer's name.
Build with Cloud Build configured to generate signed build provenance, store images in Artifact Registry, and share the provenance with customers.
Cloud Build can generate signed SLSA build provenance describing the source and build process, which customers can verify.
README files, logs on shared drives, and name tags aren't tamper-resistant or verifiable.

A data ingestion service calls several Google Cloud APIs at high volume and occasionally receives HTTP 429 and 503 errors. The current code retries immediately in a tight loop, which worsens the problem. What should the architect advise?
Fail the request permanently on the first error.
Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter, respect retry limits, and make operations idempotent where possible.
Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries over time and reduces contention, and idempotency makes retries safe.
Tight retry loops amplify overload, failing immediately loses transient-recoverable work, and unlimited quota isn't available.

A service must call a third-party shipping API that allows at most 50 requests per second. Requests are generated in bursts of thousands, and each must eventually be delivered with retries. What should the architect advise?
Enqueue requests in Cloud Tasks with a queue configured for a maximum dispatch rate and retry policy, targeting an HTTP handler that calls the API.
Publish requests to Pub/Sub with push delivery and no rate control.
Call the API directly from each request handler as fast as possible.
Store requests in Cloud Storage and process them manually.
Cloud Tasks provides explicit dispatch rate limits and retries per task, matching strict rate limits on downstream APIs.
Pub/Sub push without rate control can exceed the limit, direct calls cause throttling, and manual processing doesn't scale.

A new customer-facing platform is scheduled for go-live in two weeks. Features are complete, but the operations team hasn't seen the system, and no one has tested failover or load. What should the architect require before approving go-live?
Launch as scheduled and address issues as they arise.
A production readiness review covering load and failover test results, security review sign-off, monitoring and alerting, runbooks, and an on-call rotation with trained operators.
A code freeze with no other activities.
A readiness review verifies that the system can be operated reliably and securely, including tested failure scenarios and prepared operators.
Launching without readiness risks outages, demos don't prove operability, and a code freeze alone doesn't address operational gaps.

Two years after a system was built, new engineers keep questioning why it uses Bigtable instead of BigQuery and regional rather than multi-regional deployment. No one remembers the reasoning, and teams waste time relitigating decisions. What should the architect have put in place?
Architecture Decision Records documenting each significant decision's context, options considered, rationale, and consequences, stored with the code.
Comments in the Terraform code only.
ADRs capture why decisions were made and what trade-offs were accepted, providing durable, searchable context.
Code comments and diagrams show what exists rather than why, and recordings are hard to search.

Before launch, a security team plans a penetration test of the company's applications running on Google Cloud. A manager believes they must first obtain written approval from Google. What should the architect advise?
Google must approve all penetration tests in advance.
Penetration tests are prohibited on Google Cloud.
No advance notification to Google is required for testing your own projects, but tests must comply with the Acceptable Use Policy and Terms of Service and target only resources you own.
Tests may only be performed by Google employees.
Google doesn't require customers to notify it before penetration testing their own resources, provided they follow the AUP and terms and don't target other customers or Google infrastructure.

A team wants to validate that each release can handle 50,000 concurrent users before promotion to production. It needs a scalable, repeatable load test that runs as part of the release pipeline against a staging environment. What should the architect recommend?
Ask employees to use the application simultaneously.
Run a load tool from a single developer laptop.
Test against production during peak hours.
Run distributed load tests (for example, Locust workers on GKE) from the pipeline against a production-like staging environment, with pass/fail thresholds on latency and error rates.
Distributed load generation on GKE can scale to realistic traffic, and pipeline thresholds make results actionable and repeatable.
Manual tests and single laptops can't generate enough load, and testing production at peak risks customer impact.
QA teams want production-like data in staging to reproduce real issues, but production data contains customer PII governed by privacy regulations. What should the architect recommend?
Copy production data to staging as-is and restrict access.
Create de-identified staging datasets using Sensitive Data Protection transformations such as masking, tokenization, or date shifting, preserving data shape and referential integrity where needed.
Give QA access to production directly.
De-identification produces realistic data for testing without exposing PII, and techniques like deterministic tokenization preserve relationships.
Raw copies and production access create privacy risk, and tiny synthetic data often misses real-world issues.

Twelve teams independently release microservices that call each other's APIs. Integration failures are frequently discovered only in production when a provider changes a response field that a consumer depends on. What should the architect recommend?
Consumer-driven contract testing in each service's CI pipeline, so that providers verify they still satisfy consumers' published expectations before release.
A monthly full end-to-end test of all services together.
Merge all services into one repository and one release.
Contract tests catch breaking changes at build time without requiring all services to be deployed together.
Monthly end-to-end tests find problems too late, freezing APIs blocks evolution, and a single release reintroduces monolithic coupling.

A development team is handing over a new payment service to a central SRE team for operation. The SRE team refuses to accept it without better operational documentation. What should the architect ensure is delivered?
Only the source code repository link.
A list of team members' phone numbers.
Runbooks for common alerts and failure scenarios, architecture and dependency documentation, SLOs and dashboards, escalation paths, and backup and restore procedures.
Operational documentation such as runbooks, SLOs, dependencies, escalation paths, and recovery procedures enables another team to run the service safely.
Source code and contact lists aren't operational guidance, and customer manuals don't cover operations.

A platform team publishes shared Terraform modules used by 40 application teams. A recent module change passed code review but broke network configurations for several teams when they upgraded. What should the architect recommend to improve module readiness?
Stop versioning modules so all teams always get the latest.
Allow only the platform team to use the modules.
Require manual testing by each consuming team.

Add automated module tests (for example, `terraform validate`, plan checks, and `terraform test` or integration tests that deploy into ephemeral test projects), publish semantic versions, and let teams pin versions.
Automated testing in ephemeral environments catches breaking changes before release, and semantic versioning with pinning lets consumers upgrade deliberately.
Unversioned modules spread breaking changes, restricting use defeats the purpose, and manual testing by every team is inefficient.

A release passed all tests in staging but failed in production because production used a different Cloud SQL tier, different firewall rules, and a manually added configuration flag. What should the architect recommend?
Test only in production from now on.

Define staging and production from the same infrastructure-as-code modules with environment-specific variables, keep configuration in version control, and detect drift so environments stay consistent.
Make staging smaller to save costs, regardless of differences.
Add more manual steps to the production deployment checklist.
Shared IaC with explicit parameters and drift detection keeps environments consistent, so staging results predict production behavior.
Testing only in production is risky, unmanaged differences undermine testing, and manual steps introduce more drift.

A company is launching a new recommendation feature that will call a new backend service for every page view. The team is unsure whether the backend can handle full production traffic and wants to validate it with real traffic before users see the feature. What should the architect recommend?

A dark launch: send real production requests to the new backend in the background (with results discarded or hidden behind a feature flag) to measure performance and errors before enabling the feature for users.
Test with synthetic traffic in development only.
Delay launch until the next major release.
Dark launches expose the backend to real production load without affecting user experience, revealing capacity issues safely.
Immediate full launch risks user-facing failures, synthetic development tests may not represent production, and delaying doesn't validate readiness.

An on-call team receives dozens of pages per week from alerts on high CPU and memory on individual VMs, but most pages don't correspond to any customer impact. Meanwhile, a real outage last month was noticed first by customers. The service has a 99.9% availability SLO. What alerting approach should the architect recommend?
Lower CPU alert thresholds so issues are caught earlier.
Add more resource-level alerts for disk and network.

Alert on SLO error budget burn rate using multiple windows (for example, a fast burn over one hour and a slow burn over several hours), and move resource metrics to dashboards or non-paging notifications.
Remove all alerts and rely on customer reports.
Burn-rate alerts page only when user-facing reliability is at risk, catching real outages quickly while ignoring harmless resource spikes.
Lower thresholds and more resource alerts increase noise, and relying on customers delays response.

A company wants to track a service's 99.95% availability SLO over a rolling 28-day window, visualize remaining error budget, and alert when the budget is being consumed too quickly, using Google Cloud's native tools. What should the architect configure?
Define the service and its SLO in Cloud Monitoring (SLO monitoring) using load balancer request metrics as the SLI, and create burn-rate alerting policies on the SLO.
Export logs to BigQuery and calculate availability manually each month.
Build a spreadsheet updated by on-call engineers.
Cloud Monitoring's SLO monitoring computes SLI compliance and error budget over rolling windows and supports burn-rate alerts.
Manual BigQuery calculations and spreadsheets are slow and error-prone, and an uptime check alone doesn't track an error budget from real user traffic.
An SRE team is overwhelmed by 300 alerts per day, many of which are duplicates or informational. Engineers have started ignoring pages, and burnout is high. What should the architect recommend?
Hire more on-call engineers to handle the volume.
Page for every alert, but only during business hours.
Mute all alerts for a month.
Review alerts so that paging is reserved for urgent, actionable, user-impacting symptoms; route non-urgent issues to tickets; deduplicate related alerts; and delete alerts that never lead to action.
Good alerting pages only for actionable, urgent symptoms, which reduces fatigue and improves response to real incidents.
More engineers don't fix noisy alerts, business-hours paging ignores real incidents at night, and muting everything hides outages.
A team launching a new user-facing API asks which signals they should put on their primary service dashboard to quickly understand its health. What should the architect recommend?
VM uptime and number of deployments.
The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
Daily cost and number of log entries.
The golden signals capture user experience (latency, errors) along with demand and resource pressure (traffic, saturation).
VM uptime, CPU alone, cost, and log counts give an incomplete view of service health.

Developers struggle to find application exceptions buried in millions of log lines from Cloud Run and GKE services. They want new error types grouped automatically, with counts, stack traces, first-seen times, and notifications. What should the architect recommend?
Create one log-based metric per possible exception type.
Use Error Reporting, which aggregates and groups errors from logs and can notify on new error groups.
Error Reporting groups similar exceptions, tracks occurrences and stack traces, and notifies on new errors.
Longer retention doesn't organize errors, predefining metrics for unknown exceptions isn't feasible, and flow logs don't capture application errors.

An e-commerce company's uptime checks show the homepage is up, yet customers occasionally can't complete checkout because a login-to-cart-to-payment flow breaks. The company wants to detect broken multi-step user journeys proactively. What should the architect recommend?
Cloud Monitoring synthetic monitors that run scripted multi-step journeys (for example, login, add to cart, checkout) on a schedule and alert on failures.
More uptime checks on the homepage.
CPU alerts on the payment servers.
Synthetic monitors run scripted tests that exercise critical user flows end to end and alert when they fail.
Homepage checks don't validate deeper flows, CPU metrics don't prove functionality, and quarterly testing is far too infrequent.
The security team wants an immediate alert whenever anyone grants the Owner role on any production project. The event appears in Cloud Audit Logs. What should the architect configure?
A daily report of IAM policies.
An uptime check against the IAM API.
A log-based alerting policy matching `SetIamPolicy` audit log entries whose binding deltas add `roles/owner`, with notifications to the security channel.
Log-based alerting policies trigger on matching log entries, enabling near-real-time notification of specific audit events.
Daily reports are delayed, and CPU alerts or uptime checks don't detect IAM changes.

A company runs workloads on Google Cloud and AWS. Its SRE team wants a single operations view in Cloud Monitoring that includes metrics from EC2 instances and other AWS services alongside Google Cloud resources. What should the architect recommend?
Build separate dashboards in each cloud and switch between them.
Configure Cloud Monitoring to collect AWS metrics through an AWS connector project (and install the Ops Agent on EC2 instances for guest metrics).
Export AWS logs to Cloud Storage weekly.
Use VPC Flow Logs for AWS.
Cloud Monitoring can ingest AWS metrics through an AWS connector, and the Ops Agent can collect guest-level telemetry, providing a unified view.
Separate dashboards fragment operations, weekly exports aren't real-time monitoring, and VPC Flow Logs are a Google Cloud feature.

During an outage, engineers spent an hour debugging their own application before discovering that a Google Cloud service in their region was experiencing an incident. The company wants to be notified automatically about Google Cloud incidents that affect its projects. What should the architect configure?
Subscribe engineers to a general cloud news newsletter.
Check the public status dashboard manually during incidents.
Personalized Service Health, with alerts for incidents affecting the company's projects and services routed to on-call channels.
Personalized Service Health reports Google Cloud incidents relevant to your projects and can send alerts, shortening diagnosis.
Newsletters and manual dashboard checks are slow and generic, and more logging doesn't reveal provider incidents.

A product team keeps shipping features rapidly, but its service has exhausted its quarterly error budget after several release-related incidents. Product managers want to keep releasing at the same pace. What should the architect recommend according to SRE practices?
Lower the SLO so that the error budget isn't exhausted.
Apply the agreed error budget policy: pause non-essential feature releases and prioritize reliability work until the service is back within budget.
Ignore the error budget until the next quarter.
Double the release frequency to fix bugs faster.
An error budget policy balances velocity and reliability; when the budget is spent, teams shift effort to reliability.
Lowering the SLO to fit poor performance undermines its purpose, ignoring the budget makes it meaningless, and more releases increase risk.

A company deploys to GKE through Cloud Deploy using canary rollouts. Last week, a faulty canary ran for hours before someone noticed elevated errors. The company wants canaries to be evaluated and rolled back automatically. What should the architect recommend?
Remove canary stages to speed up deployments.
Ask engineers to watch dashboards during every rollout.

Configure deployment verification that checks key metrics (such as error rate and latency) during the canary phase, and use Cloud Deploy automation to roll back or stop promotion when verification fails.
Automated verification against SLO-related metrics catches bad canaries quickly, and automation can roll back without human delay.
A larger canary increases impact, removing canaries removes protection, and manual watching is unreliable.

A global outage occurred when a configuration change, a new feature flag value, was pushed to all regions at once. Application code releases already use progressive rollouts, but configuration changes don't. What should the architect recommend?
Treat configuration changes like code: roll them out progressively by region or percentage with validation and automated rollback, rather than pushing globally at once.
Push configuration changes only on weekends.
Store configuration in environment variables baked into images.
Progressive, validated rollouts limit the blast radius of configuration changes, just as they do for code.
Banning changes blocks the business, weekend pushes don't reduce blast radius, and baking configuration into images removes the flexibility of runtime flags.

Thirty minutes after a release, error rates rise sharply. The on-call engineer thinks they know the bug and wants to write and deploy a fix. The previous version is known to be healthy and can be restored in two minutes. What should the architect recommend as the default practice?
Deploy the new fix immediately without testing.
Wait until the next business day to decide.
Roll back to the last known-good version first to restore service, then investigate and deploy a tested fix.
Scale up the new version to handle errors.
Rolling back to a known-good release mitigates user impact fastest and with the least risk, leaving time for proper diagnosis.
Untested fixes can make things worse, waiting prolongs the outage, and scaling doesn't fix bugs.

A company releases once per quarter with hundreds of changes per release, and each release causes multi-day incidents. Leadership fears that releasing more often would increase instability. What should the architect advise?
Release even less often, twice a year, to reduce disruptions.
Move toward smaller, more frequent releases with automated testing and progressive delivery, and measure DORA metrics such as change failure rate and time to restore.
Require executive sign-off for every change.
Freeze development until all bugs are fixed.
Smaller releases reduce risk per change, simplify troubleshooting, and, with automation, improve both speed and stability as measured by DORA metrics.
Less frequent releases make batches larger and riskier, heavy approvals slow delivery without improving quality, and freezes halt value delivery.

During GKE node upgrades and application rollouts, a critical service sometimes has all its replicas terminated at once, and traffic reaches Pods that haven't finished starting. What should the architect recommend?
Run a single replica to simplify operations.
Increase the node pool size only.
Configure PodDisruptionBudgets to keep a minimum number of replicas available during voluntary disruptions, and add readiness probes so traffic reaches only Pods ready to serve.
PodDisruptionBudgets limit simultaneous voluntary evictions, and readiness probes prevent routing to Pods that aren't ready.
Disabling upgrades leaves clusters unpatched, a single replica removes redundancy, and more nodes don't control eviction behavior.
6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management
During a recent major outage, ten engineers debugged simultaneously, customers received conflicting updates, and nobody tracked decisions. What should the architect recommend for future incidents?
Adopt a structured incident management process with defined roles—incident commander, operations lead, and communications lead—a shared incident document, and regular status updates.
Have the most senior engineer handle everything alone.
Let everyone work independently and share results at the end.
Wait for the problem to resolve itself before communicating.
Clear incident roles coordinate response, separate communication from debugging, and maintain a record of decisions.
One person doing everything becomes a bottleneck, uncoordinated work causes confusion, and silence damages customer trust.
6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management

After an outage caused by a misconfigured load balancer, management wants to find who made the mistake and discipline them. The architect is concerned this will discourage honest reporting. What should the architect recommend?
Skip the review to avoid conflict.
Conduct a blameless postmortem that focuses on the timeline, contributing factors, and systemic fixes (such as automation and guardrails), with tracked action items.
Add more manual approvals to all changes.
Blameless postmortems encourage candor and focus on improving systems and processes so similar failures don't recur.
Blame discourages reporting, skipping reviews loses learning, and blanket manual approvals slow delivery without addressing root causes.
6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management

A global bank running mission-critical workloads on Google Cloud needs the fastest response times for critical issues, proactive guidance, and a named technical contact who knows its architecture. Which support option should the architect recommend?
Premium Support, which includes the fastest response for critical cases and a Technical Account Manager.
Premium Support offers the fastest critical-case response and a dedicated Technical Account Manager for proactive guidance.
Basic and Standard support don't provide those response levels or a named contact, and documentation isn't support.
6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management

A production outage appears to be caused by unexpected behavior in a Google Cloud managed service. The engineer opening a support case wants it resolved as quickly as possible. What should the case include?
A single sentence saying "the service is broken."
Only a screenshot of the console.
Credentials so that support can log in to the company's accounts.
The appropriate priority reflecting business impact, affected project IDs and resources, exact timestamps with time zones, error messages, steps to reproduce, and troubleshooting already performed.
Detailed, specific information about impact, resources, timing, errors, and prior troubleshooting lets support diagnose quickly.
Vague descriptions and screenshots slow resolution, and sharing credentials violates security practices.
6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management

An SRE team spends about 70% of its time on repetitive manual tasks such as restarting stuck jobs, rotating certificates by hand, and resizing disks, leaving little time for engineering improvements. What should the architect recommend?
Identify and automate high-volume toil (for example, auto-remediation, managed certificates, and autoscaling), and cap toil so that a significant share of time goes to engineering work.
Accept the toil as part of operations.
Hire contractors to perform the manual tasks.
Reduce monitoring so fewer tasks are generated.
SRE practice limits toil (commonly to under 50% of time) and invests in automation that eliminates repetitive work.
Accepting or outsourcing toil doesn't reduce it, and less monitoring hides problems rather than resolving them.
6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management

A microservices platform is designed to tolerate dependency failures with retries, timeouts, and fallbacks, but these mechanisms have never been exercised. The architect wants confidence that the system behaves as designed when dependencies fail. What should the architect recommend?
Wait for a real outage to validate behavior.

Run controlled chaos experiments, such as injecting latency and errors through Cloud Service Mesh fault injection or terminating instances, starting in staging and expanding carefully with clear abort conditions.
Chaos engineering verifies resilience mechanisms under controlled failure conditions, revealing gaps before real incidents.
Waiting for outages is risky, code review can't prove runtime behavior, and more replicas don't test fallback logic.
6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management

A company documented a regional disaster recovery plan with an RTO of one hour, but it has never been executed. Auditors ask for evidence that the RTO is achievable. What should the architect recommend?
Provide the written DR plan as evidence.
Schedule regular DR drills that perform a real or simulated regional failover, measure the achieved RTO and RPO, and update runbooks and automation based on findings.
Increase the documented RTO to four hours.
Assume managed services handle DR automatically.
Only exercised failovers prove that recovery objectives can be met and reveal gaps in runbooks and automation.
A document isn't evidence of capability, changing the target avoids the question, and managed services don't automatically fail over entire applications.

A company's defect escape rate to production is high. Code reviews are inconsistent, and tests are run manually when engineers remember. What should the architect recommend to improve quality control?
Add a manual QA sign-off at the end of each quarter.
Rely on production monitoring to catch defects.
Reduce the number of tests to speed up builds.
Enforce automated quality gates in CI, such as required unit and integration tests, static analysis, dependency and vulnerability scanning, and mandatory code review before merge.
Automated quality gates catch defects consistently before changes reach production.
Quarterly manual sign-off is too late and infrequent, monitoring detects problems after users are affected, and fewer tests reduce coverage.
After six months of reliability initiatives, leadership asks whether the investments have improved operations. What should the architect use to evaluate this objectively?
Trends in SLO attainment, error budget consumption, incident frequency and severity, mean time to detect, and mean time to restore compared with the baseline.
The number of new monitoring dashboards created.
The number of engineers on the SRE team.
The total number of alerts sent.
Outcome metrics like SLO attainment, incident rates, and detection and recovery times show whether reliability improved.
Dashboard counts, headcount, and alert volume measure activity rather than results.

Deployments complete successfully in the pipeline, but twice this month the newly deployed service was broken because of a missing secret, discovered only when customers complained. What should the architect add to the release process?
A manual customer survey after each release.
Automated post-deployment smoke tests that exercise critical endpoints immediately after deployment, failing the release and triggering rollback if they fail.
Smoke tests verify that the deployed service actually works, catching configuration errors like missing secrets before customers are affected.
Timeouts don't validate functionality, surveys are slow, and less frequent deployment doesn't prevent the issue.

A service runs in two regions, each normally using about 70% of its capacity. The business requires the service to keep meeting its SLO if one region fails. The architect is reviewing capacity plans. What should the architect conclude?
The current capacity is sufficient because average utilization is below 100%.

The plan is insufficient: if one region fails, the other would need about 140% of its capacity, so capacity (or autoscaling limits and quotas) must provide N+1 headroom to absorb a full regional failover.
Capacity planning isn't needed with autoscaling.
Reduce each region to 50% capacity to save money.
Surviving the loss of one region requires the remaining region to carry the full load, so headroom, autoscaling limits, and quotas must support it.
Average utilization below 100% doesn't guarantee failover capacity, autoscaling is bounded by quotas and capacity, and reducing capacity worsens the problem.

An e-commerce homepage fails completely whenever the personalized recommendations service is slow or down, even though customers could still browse and buy without recommendations. What design change should the architect recommend?
Make the recommendations service a single large VM.
Increase the homepage timeout to 60 seconds.
Implement graceful degradation: call recommendations with tight timeouts and a circuit breaker, and fall back to cached or default content when the service is unavailable.
Graceful degradation keeps core functionality available when non-critical dependencies fail, and circuit breakers prevent cascading slowdowns.
A larger VM doesn't remove the dependency, longer timeouts worsen user experience, and removing the feature sacrifices value.

A company's platform has grown over three years, and leadership wants a structured, periodic review to identify reliability, security, cost, and operational gaps against Google-recommended practices. What should the architect use?

Review the architecture against the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework (Architecture Framework) pillars, such as reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence, and performance, and track remediation items.
